This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ be an increasing sequence such that $a_n/n\to \infty$. Is the sum\[\sum_n \frac{a_n}{2^{a_n}}\]irrational?
#260: [Er74b][ErGr80][Er81h,p.180][Er88c,p.103][Va99,1.33]
irrationality
Erdős [Er81l] proved this is true under either of the stronger assumptions that
 $a_{n+1}-a_n\to \infty$ or 
 $a_n \gg n\sqrt{\log n\log\log n}$.
Erdős and Graham speculate that the condition $\limsup a_{n+1}-a_n=\infty$ is not sufficient, but know of no example.
In [Va99] this is asked with $a_n/n\to \infty$ replaced by $a_{n+1}-a_n\to \infty$, which as above was proved by Erdős in [Er81l].

 I would like to share a polynomial generalization of the result for Erdős Problem 260. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24972v4
Let $b\geq 2$ be an integer, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}[X]$ be nonzero, and let $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ be infinite. If
$$
\sum_{n\in S}\frac{p(n)}{b^n}\in\mathbb{Q},
$$
then, for every $0<\theta\leq 1$, there exist constants $c>0$ and $N_0$ such that
$$
\#\bigl(S\cap(N,N+W]\bigr)\geq cW
$$
whenever
$$
N\geq N_0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
N^\theta\leq W\leq N.
$$
In particular, rationality forces $S$ to have positive lower density. If $d=\deg p$, every sufficiently large gap of length $g$ beginning at $x$ satisfies
$$
g\leq d\log_b x+O(1).
$$
Consequently, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$
g\leq x^\varepsilon
$$
for all sufficiently large $x$. Thus, zero lower density—or an unbounded enumeration ratio—implies irrationality of the corresponding series. The specialization $b=2$ and $p(X)=X$ recovers the original Erdős Problem 260 statement.
A Lean 4/Mathlib formalization, implemented and audited with substantial assistance from OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, is available at:
https://github.com/Hanziwww/erdos260
The new development is located in 'Erdos260/PolynomialWindow/'.
I am especially grateful to Stijn Cambie, whose simplification of the earlier proof isolated its essential mechanism. That simplification was a crucial prerequisite for this polynomial generalization.

 If $a \in \mathbb{N}$, $b \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$, and $A$ is the set of all numbers of the form $am + b$ (with $m$ a positive integer), then
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{n \in A} \frac{n}{2^n} = \sum_m \frac{am + b}{2^{am + b}} = \left(\frac{1}{2^b}\right)\left(\frac{a2^a}{(2^a - 1)^2}\right) + \left(\frac{b}{2^b}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2^a - 1}\right).
\end{equation*}
In particular, this number is rational. To see this, first observe that
\begin{equation*}
\sum_m \frac{am + b}{2^{am + b}} = \frac{1}{2^b}\sum_m \frac{am + b}{2^{am}}
\end{equation*}
\begin{equation*}
= \frac{1}{2^b}\sum_m \frac{am}{2^{am}} + \frac{1}{2^b}\sum_m \frac{b}{2^{am}}
\end{equation*}
\begin{equation*}
= \left(\frac{1}{2^b}\right)\sum_m \frac{am}{2^{am}} + \left(\frac{b}{2^b}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2^a - 1}\right).
\end{equation*}
Now all that remains is to prove that
\begin{equation*}
\sum_m \frac{am}{2^{am}} = \frac{a2^a}{(2^a - 1)^2}.
\end{equation*}
To see this, recall that
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{1 - x^a} = \sum_m x^{am}
\end{equation*}
for all $x \in (-1, 1)$. The desired result is obtained by differentiating with respect to $x$, multiplying by $x$, and then setting $x = \frac{1}{2}$.
(Note that this argument for $A = \mathbb{N}$ is already well-known; see, for example, this StackExchange post.)

A full proof 
claimed by Han Wang (using using GPT-5.5 for auditing, language editing, restructuring, and assistance with parts of the Lean development).
 Summary:
 The paper proves that if the sum of n / 2^n over an infinite set S is rational, then S must contain a fixed positive proportion of the integers in every large interval from X to 2X. Erdős Problem 260 follows because the condition a_n / n -> infinity makes the set {a_n} too sparse for this to happen.
The proof converts rationality into strong restrictions on the tails of the series. If one of these intervals were sparse, many repeated patterns would appear among the gaps in S. Those repetitions force the associated tail values into a rigid structure, making them too few to account for the amount of sparsity assumed. This contradiction gives the result.
